newsitem.title: CHINA: China warns Fiji on official relations with Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: China warns Fiji on official relations with Taiwan.

text.p: China on Thursday said it had made representations to Fiji over a visit by its president to diplomatic rival Taiwan and warned against any official relations with the island it regards as a rebel province.
"We have already made representations to Fiji," Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a news briefing when asked to comment on Fiji President Kamisese Mara's visit to Taiwan.
"Any country that develops any form of official relations with Taiwan will only be hurting its bilateral relations with China," Shen said.
Mara arrived in Taiwan on Thursday for a six-day official visit and was scheduled to meet Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui on Friday.
Fiji inked a mutual-recognition pact with Taiwan in October, drawing a warning from China not to fall for ploys by Taipei to break free of its diplomatic isolation.
Taiwan's Foreign Minister John Chang has said Taiwan would push for full diplomatic relations with Fiji, a former British territory in the South Pacific.
Beijing has regarded Nationalist-held Taiwan as a renegade province since the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949 and refuses to recognise any country having official relations with the island.
China scored a big victory in its quest to isolate Taiwan when South Africa said in November it would switch recognition to Beijing from Taipei by the end of 1997.
Pretoria's decision would reduce the number of countries that have official relations with Taiwan to 29 -- mostly impoverished states in Africa and central America.
Aside from Fiji, Taipei maintains mutual recognition pacts with two other Pacific islands that recognise Beijing -- Vanuatu and Papua New Guinea.
Taiwan has provided agricultural assistance to Fiji since 1978 and opened a trade office there in 1987.
